SCOPe puts the catalytic (nucleotide-binding) domains of actin/HSP70, hexokinase and glycerol kinase in the same superfamily, the actin-like ATPase domain superfamily (c.55.1). This sits in the ribonuclease H-like motif fold (c.55) of the alpha/beta class (c). Each protein has its own family within that superfamily: the actin/HSP70 family, the hexokinase family and the glycerol kinase family. I am not fully sure of the exact family-level sccs numbers. The superfamily placement means SCOPe sees structural and functional evidence for a common evolutionary origin despite low sequence similarity. The signs are a conserved two-lobe core, each lobe with an RNase H-like beta-sheet and helices, a nucleotide-binding cleft between the lobes, and conserved phosphate-binding motifs. The separate families mean the relationship is remote homology, not close orthology.

This permits several inferences. The domains descend from a common ancestor. They share the core architecture, including the two-lobe topology, the ATP-binding cleft and the hinge-like domain closure. A structure from one family can serve as a fold-level template, and the conserved ATP/phosphate-binding site can be located by superposition. Remote-homology searches can also be justified on this basis.

It does not permit transferring detailed function. Actin is a structural, polymerizing ATPase. HSP70 is a chaperone whose ATPase cycle is coupled to substrate binding. Hexokinase phosphorylates hexoses and glycerol kinase phosphorylates glycerol, so the substrates and chemistry differ. Superfamily membership therefore does not justify inferring substrate specificity, EC number, kinase activity, regulation, oligomerization or cellular role, and it does not justify inferring the specific active-site residues. Homology-model accuracy is also limited. Loops, insertions, subdomain orientation and the open or closed state differ between families, so a template from another family gives only a rough core model. A same-family relationship with experimental support would be needed for stronger function transfer. Homology at the superfamily level is also not the same as the fold level. Fold-level similarity alone does not imply common ancestry, which here rests on the superfamily assignment.
